# Review — single-lens

## Overview

This skill is the **single-lens code review**. One reviewer agent reads the whole
diff a bead produced — implementation **and** tests together — and emits one
triage verdict.

The cost model is "one strong reviewer instead of a panel": the formula pins
this step to the strongest model precisely because there is no panel behind it
to catch what the single lens misses.

The output is a fenced ```json``` triage sidecar, so the loop gate (`djinn.check.review_approved` via
`ParseTriageSidecar`) routes it with no special-casing — including the
BLOCKER-count gate, the citation ground-truth gate, and the invented-rate gate.

## The single-lens rule — no fan-out

**You are the reviewer. You do the review yourself.** Fanning out would
reinstate the exact multi-agent cost this skill exists to cut, which is the
whole point of the step. So, absolutely:

- Do **NOT** invoke any other review skill or command to do the review for you.
- Do **NOT** delegate any part of the review to a `Task` / `Agent` subagent —
  not for evidence-gathering, not for a "second opinion", not to parallelize the
  rubric below.

One agent, one pass, one sidecar. If the diff is large, read more of it — do not
split it across helpers.

Two more hard rules, symmetric with every other review path:

- **Do not modify code.** No edits, no fixes, no "while I was in there". The
  loop's paired fix step applies findings on the next iteration.
- **Do not write files.** The sidecar goes in your visible response text.

## Inputs

The invoker provides:

1. **The bead, in a `<bead>` block** — its id, title, description,
   acceptance_criteria, design and notes, copied verbatim from the tracker by
   the invoker. Judge the bead from that block alone. Run no `bd` command: a
   reviewer may run in a sandbox with no beads database, and the block is the
   bead as the invoker read it. The `acceptance_criteria` lines are what the
   completeness concern below is scored against — one `criteria` row each.
2. **The diff to review** — either an explicit base ref, or the
   pre-implementation baseline. Absent an explicit base, reconstruct it:
   `git diff <base>..HEAD` (plus `git status` / `git diff` for uncommitted work).
   Every promoted fix finding must cite a `file:line` that lands inside this
   diff — the harness ground-truths citations against exactly this range.

3. **The round's scope, under `## Scope of this round`** — `full`,
   `spot-check` or `fix`. It decides which diff you sweep; see Step 1. Absent,
   treat the round as `full`.

   **On iteration 2 and later, extra blocks** — "What iteration N-1
   found" (the previous pass's promoted findings), "What the last fix
   changed" (`git diff <that review's SHA>..HEAD`), on a `fix` round
   `## Criteria rows from round N-1`, and `## Findings the fix step declined`
   when the fix step declined any finding. They are the incremental half of
   this review; see "Answering the previous iteration" below. On iteration 1
   none of them is present and there is nothing to answer.

4. **The bead's comments, under `## Evidence on the bead`** — every comment on
   the bead, oldest first, each a `### <author> <time>` heading over its body,
   read by the invoker when it built this prompt. Proof a worker posted as a
   bead comment (timings, capture paths, measurement runs) lives here, and
   so do the harness's `djinn-evidence` records of earlier passes. A
   `djinn design review` verdict comment arrives without its P3/P4 polish
   section: polish is never a code-review concern. The block is absent when
   the bead has no comments.

5. **The full test suite, under `## Test suite`** — the module's full test
   command (`go test -short ./...`, or the repo's configured command), run by
   the harness outside your sandbox on this iteration's tree before you: the
   revision it ran against, the exact command, its exit code, each failing
   test's `--- FAIL:` name and package, and the output tail. Read the
   full-suite result from this block. Inside a sandbox part of the suite
   cannot run (a test that execs `ps`, a test that writes a git index under
   the temp dir), so a module-wide `go test ./...` of your own verifies only
   part of it: never run one. When you need to run tests yourself, run only
   the packages the diff touches. The block is absent only when the harness
   ran no suite (a dry run); then cite none.

6. **The approved design note, under `## The approved design note`** — the
   plan a design reviewer of the other model family approved before any code
   was written. The implementer builds to it and may depart from it only with a
   stated reason: a `Design departure: <what changed> — <why>` line in the
   message body of the commit that departs, which you read in
   `git log <base>..HEAD`. The block is absent when the formula ran no design
   step; then the design rule below does not apply. The note never replaces the
   acceptance criteria: they stay what concern 2 scores. After it may come
   `## Points the design review left to you`: the points the design review
   graded P2, each with its id, which the implementer had to settle.

If the prompt carries no `<bead>` block, stop and say so — a review with no
acceptance criteria in hand cannot be scored.

## Answering the previous iteration

The review loop is a conversation, not a series of independent samples. When
the two blocks above are present, your sidecar MUST answer them — the harness
computes the loop's progress from your answers, and a pass that ignores them
reads as a loop that is making none.

**For each finding the previous iteration promoted**, emit one `prior_findings`
entry — `{"file", "line", "status"}` — echoing the `file` and `line` exactly as
the block wrote them, so the harness can match your entry to the finding:

- `"status": "resolved"` — the fix landed; this is no longer true of the code.
- `"status": "unresolved"` — still true, whether the fix missed it, only
  half-applied it, or made it worse.

Check the code, not the fix diff's intent. A fix that edited the cited line
without addressing the finding is `unresolved`.

**For each finding under `## Findings the fix step declined`**, rule on the
decline. The fix step changed no code for it and gave evidence (a `file:line`,
a test name, or command output) that the finding is wrong. Open that evidence
yourself, then emit one `prior_findings` entry at the finding's `file` and
`line`, with a one-sentence `reason`:

- `"status": "upheld"` — the evidence does not refute the finding: it is still
  true of the code. Upheld counts as unresolved: re-promote the finding as a
  `promoted_findings` row at the same `file` and `line`, with an `action` that
  answers the fix step's evidence. The fix step may not decline it again.
- `"status": "withdrawn"` — the evidence shows the finding was wrong (the cited
  test already covers the case, the path cannot be reached, the code does not
  do what the finding said). It closes; do not re-promote it.

Rule on whether the finding is true, never on what fixing it costs. A decline
whose reason is cost, effort or a disagreement with the grade is no evidence:
uphold it, and grade the re-promoted row under Step 3 like any other finding.
A declined finding gets `upheld` or `withdrawn`, never `resolved` or
`unresolved`; omitting its entry reads as `upheld`.

**On a `fix` round, carry the criteria rows forward.** For each row under
`## Criteria rows from round N-1`, copy it into your `criteria` array unchanged
unless the fix diff changes the code the row cites, or the row was `partial` or
`fail`; re-judge those rows against the code now. Every acceptance line still
gets exactly one row.

**Every `unresolved` entry MUST also be re-promoted** as a `promoted_findings`
row at the same `file` and `line`, with the severity it still deserves and an
`action` describing what is left to do. The `prior_findings` entry is your
verdict on the last fix; the promoted row is the work order. The harness
carries an unresolved prior finding forward on your behalf if you omit the row,
for as many passes as it survives — but it can only carry the wording of the
reviewer who first raised it, which is a description of the code before any of
these fixes touched it. Re-promoting is how the
fixer learns what the half-applied fix actually left behind. Do not use the
`prior_findings` entry alone as a way to say "still broken" and move on.

**A re-promotion is not a NEW finding.** `origin` describes findings this pass
raised for the first time; the harness knows every citation the loop has been
carrying — not just the last pass's — and ignores any `origin` you put on one of
those, so you cannot accidentally get a re-promoted row filed away as a
follow-up instead of fixed.
Tag it or don't — the row goes back to the fix step either way.

**For each NEW finding you promote**, add an `origin`:

- `"origin": "regression"` — the fix diff introduced it. Something in "What the
  last fix changed" is the reason this finding is true.
- `"origin": "latent"` — it pre-existed that fix. This pass is simply the first
  to look there.

Judge origin from the fix diff, not from how serious the finding feels. The two
are not the same claim and the harness treats them differently:

- A **regression** is the loop's own damage. It keeps the loop iterating.
- A **latent IMPORTANT** is filed as a P2 follow-up bead and is NOT handed to the
  fix step. The bead is tracked; the loop moves on.
- A **BLOCKER** blocks either way. `latent` buys it nothing.

So mislabeling a latent finding as a regression keeps the loop open on work it
was never meant to carry — the failure that deferred a bead after three passes
each found one new IMPORTANT somewhere else. Mislabeling a real regression as
latent ships it. Neither is a safe default; read the diff.

Both bullets above are about findings that are new at this citation. A latent
IMPORTANT the loop is already carrying is not filed a second time, however many
passes ago it was raised.

Omitting `origin` means `regression` (the conservative reading), and omitting
`prior_findings` entirely means "every prior finding is still unresolved as far
as the harness can tell" — both are honest fallbacks, neither is a shortcut.

## Process

### Step 1. Read the bead, then read the diff the scope names

Read the bead first so the acceptance criteria are in hand before the code
frames your judgment. Then read `## Scope of this round`; it names the diff you
sweep:

- **`full` or `spot-check`** — the block names `git diff <claim SHA>..HEAD`,
  the bead's whole diff. Read all of it. A `spot-check` is a forced second look
  at a clean `SHIP`: sweep it exactly as a `full` round, without trusting the
  earlier pass.
- **`fix`** — the block names `git diff <review anchor>..HEAD`, the fix diff
  since the last review, and lists the open findings. Do NOT sweep the bead's
  whole diff. Review three things only: the fix diff, each open finding (is it
  resolved now?), and each declined finding (rule on it). Read the code around
  a hunk or a finding as far as you need to judge it, but raise a new finding
  only when the fix diff introduced it or it sits in code the fix diff changed.

Read the diff in scope — implementation and tests in one sitting, not as two
passes. Reviewing them together is the point: the tests are evidence about the
implementation, and the implementation is evidence about whether the tests are
vacuous.

### Step 2. Sweep the rubric

Sweep **every** concern below over the diff in scope: the whole diff on a
`full` or `spot-check` round, the fix diff on a `fix` round. Each one is a
named concern you are accountable for, not a suggestion.

**Implementation concerns**

| # | Concern | The question you answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Correctness bugs** | Bugs, nil dereferences, missing error paths, off-by-ones, unhandled failure branches. Does the code do what it says on any input, not just the happy one? |
| 2 | **Acceptance-criteria completeness** | Which of the bead's `acceptance_criteria` are **not yet represented in code**? Walk them one at a time, recording each as a `criteria` row (Step 5); a criterion with no corresponding code or test is an IMPORTANT at minimum. |
| 3 | **Simplicity / deletable code** | What could be **deleted** without breaking anything — dead branches, unused fields, a duplicated utility that already exists elsewhere in the repo, a layer of indirection carrying one caller? |
| 4 | **Behavior at scale** | What breaks at 10× the input volume the bead assumes (the bead's Scalability Assumption if it states one)? Where is the hot path, and what did this diff put on it? |
| 5 | **Adversarial-caller boundary assumptions** | Which assumptions about callers are wrong if the caller is adversarial or merely careless — unvalidated inputs, trusted-but-external data, invariants asserted in a comment instead of in code? |

**Test concerns**

| # | Concern | The question you answer |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | **Vacuously-true test assertions** | Would any assertion pass against an **empty** implementation? An assertion on a constant, on a value the test itself just set, or on "no error" alone is vacuous. Also: delete the most important line of implementation — which test catches it? If none, say so. |
| 7 | **Cheapest implementation that passes the tests** | What is the cheapest, dumbest implementation that passes every test in this diff? If shipping that would embarrass the author, the tests are underspecified — report it against the tests, not the implementation. When your prompt carries a `## Mutation check` report, every `survived` test in it passes with the bead's code change reverted: give each one exactly one disposition — a guard (it pins behaviour the diff deliberately keeps) listed under `mutation_survivors` (Step 5), or an IMPORTANT `kind: "fix"` test finding citing the test's `file:line` that says what it must assert to fail without the change. A survivor with neither is a refused review. |
| 8 | **Uncovered scenarios** | What scenario is not covered at all — error paths, empty/boundary inputs, the concurrent case? |
| 9 | **Tests coupled to implementation details** | Do any tests assert on internals (call order, private shape, log text) rather than behavior, such that a legitimate refactor breaks them? |

Concerns 1–7 are the ones this step is contractually accountable for; 8 and 9
round out the test lens.

**The design rule.** When the prompt carries `## The approved design note`,
also sweep the diff against it: its data shapes, the parts it said it would
touch and how they connect, the approach it picked, the proof it promised, and
what it said it would not do. Every place the code does something else is a
departure. Find each departure's `Design departure:` line in the commit
messages of `git log <base>..HEAD`. A departure with no such line is a
finding, graded in Step 3 below; a departure with one is judged on its merits
like any other change.

When the prompt also carries `## Points the design review left to you`, read
each point on that list: a real point the design review graded P2 and left for
the implementer to settle while building. Find where the diff settles each one.
A point the build did not settle is a finding, graded in Step 3 below like any
other.

### Step 3. Grade each finding

First decide whether the finding sits **inside the bead's intent**. The bead's
intent is the paths its description, acceptance criteria and design name, plus
every line of code those paths run — wherever it lives. A shared helper outside
the bead's named feature is inside the intent when the bead's path calls it on
an ordinary run; what decides is whether the bead's path reaches the defect,
not which file or package holds it. A path that worked before this diff and
that the diff breaks is inside the intent too. Outside it: code the diff
touches that only another feature, an operator-only or debug entry point, or a
path no criterion names runs; and a defect that predates the diff on such a
path.

Assign every finding a severity:

- **`BLOCKER`** — the change is wrong or unsafe as written: the bead's path
  gives the wrong result on the very input its acceptance criteria describe, a
  missing acceptance criterion that makes the bead false, data loss, a security
  hole, a broken invariant. A BLOCKER means the diff must not ship as-is. Data
  loss, a security hole or a broken invariant is a BLOCKER on any path. A
  defect on a failure branch of the bead's path — an error swallowed or
  misreported when a dependency times out or a lookup fails — is IMPORTANT,
  not BLOCKER, even when it yields wrong output on that branch.

  **Visual work needs its capture.** A bead whose diff changes a visual surface
  (`web/`, a terminal-UI package, a visual asset) is a BLOCKER when its evidence
  comment lacks the capture contract §4 requires, or when that capture misses an
  element the reference shows and the acceptance criteria name. Review runs
  before commit-push writes that comment, and the rule above holds here too:
  run no `bd` command for it. Look for the capture only where the invoker
  points you — the capture files the diff commits, capture artifacts in the
  worktree (`.playwright-cli/`, a saved `tmux capture-pane` text) that the
  diff or the invoker's prompt names, any implementer report or prior
  evidence the invoker pasted into your prompt, and the prompt's
  `## Evidence on the bead` block with every capture path a comment there
  names. Open each one yourself; a
  golden file alone is not the capture, and a capture no supplied source
  reaches counts as missing.
  Record each capture and its per-element comparison in that criterion's
  `criteria` row, so commit-push carries it into the evidence comment.
  **A design departure needs its reason.** Code that departs from the
  approved design note with no `Design departure:` line naming it is an
  **IMPORTANT** `fix` finding at minimum — cite the departing `file:line` and
  name what the note said; the fix is to build to the note, or to state the
  reason in a commit. It is a **BLOCKER** when the unexplained departure also
  breaks an acceptance criterion, contradicts a repo ruling, or ships what the
  note's `## Out of scope` said this bead would not do.
- **`IMPORTANT`** — a real defect a caller will hit on a path inside the bead's
  intent: wrong output, a missing or swallowed error, a panic, a scale or
  boundary hazard at the volume the bead assumes, on an input an ordinary
  caller of that path produces. Also IMPORTANT: an acceptance criterion with no
  code or test (concern 2), a meaningfully underspecified test of the bead's own
  behavior, a mutation survivor that is not a guard (concern 7), and an
  unexplained design departure (below). Name the caller and the input in the
  `action`. A defect you cannot place on the bead's path is not IMPORTANT.
- **`NIT`** — worth doing, not worth blocking on: naming, comment drift, a
  tidier arrangement, and every real defect that is not IMPORTANT under the
  rule above —
  - a defect on a path outside the bead's intent;
  - a rare case: it needs an input, timing or environment no ordinary caller of
    the bead's path produces, or a volume past the one the bead assumes;
  - a small cost: the harm is minor (an extra allocation, a redundant call, a
    misleading log line) and nothing returns a wrong result.

  These are never fixed inline; whether one becomes a follow-up bead is decided
  by the `priority` grade below. Grade a real behavior defect on another path
  or in a rare case **P2** when it is worth tracking until someone fixes it,
  so it files as a follow-up instead of being lost.
- **`INVENTED`** — reserved for the self-audit: a finding you could not anchor
  to a real `file:line` in the diff. Count it honestly rather than deleting it;
  the invented-rate is a diagnostic on the reviewer, and a silently-dropped
  invention teaches the harness nothing.

**Within NIT, grade a filing priority (`priority`).** Every promoted NIT `fix`
finding ALSO carries a `priority` grade that decides whether it becomes a
tracked backlog bead or stays report-only. The default is **P4** — anything
whose fix is more verification or polish rather than a behavior change. P4
explicitly includes pure polish, cosmetic, style, speculative-future and
test-micro-tightening findings (the canonical noise: "extract a constant", "use
`bytes.Cut`", "strengthen this assertion", "rename for clarity") **and** the
absent-verification shapes — untested error path, named-coverage gap, drift trap
between two sources. Those stay valuable as report content, but their fix is
"add a test / comment / sync", not a behavior change; graded at the filing floor
they buried the backlog under ~100 add-a-test beads (closed as a class in the
2026-08-03 triage). Grade **P3** when the NIT names a **deferred behavior defect**
— code in the diff that produces observably wrong runtime behavior (wrong
output, panic, false verdict, resource leak, silent data loss) which the fix
step is deferring rather than fixing this iteration. **P3 is report-only**: the
floor moved to P2 (operator ruling D1, 2026-09-03), so a P3-graded NIT is
dropped exactly like a P4 and stays in this sidecar for human reading. Grade
**P2 ONLY** when that deferred behavior defect is severe enough that recording
it in this sidecar is not enough — it has to be carried on the backlog until
someone fixes it. A `review-follow-up` bead has to *earn* P2; P2 is the only
grade that files. Litmus test: if the
entire fix is "add a test", "add a comment", or "sync two sources", it is P4 no
matter how real the underlying risk reads. When in doubt, **P4** — this sidecar
preserves the finding for human reading either way.

The `file_nits` filer reads this grade per-finding and files only at or above
the floor, so an ungraded NIT falls back to the filer's batch default and is
report-only. Grade explicitly when you want a finding tracked.
BLOCKER/IMPORTANT findings route to the fix step, NOT the follow-up filer, so
their `priority` is unused — omit it or leave it empty there, as for counters.

Every promoted **fix** finding MUST cite a real `file` and `line` from the diff.
A finding you cannot anchor is not a finding — either anchor it or count it as
`INVENTED`.

The one honest exception is a finding **about a caller of the changed code** —
"this changed signature breaks its three call sites", "the invariant this diff
altered is assumed here" — whose truthful citation is a file the diff never
touched. Cite the caller's real `file` and `line` and set
`"caller_of_changed_code": true`. The harness's citation gate then keeps the
finding instead of rejecting it for pointing outside the diff. Do NOT set the
flag to smuggle a citation you could not anchor: an unanchorable finding is
still `INVENTED`.

A finding that is an **anti-recommendation** ("do NOT do X", "resist the urge to
extract this") is promoted with `"kind": "counter"` rather than `"kind": "fix"`.
The fix step skips counters by contract; a counter carries no obligation to act.

A finding whose **only** fix is an action no worker may take is promoted with
`"kind": "lead"` and a `"lead_action"` from this closed list:

- `reinstall-binary` — the proof needs the installed djinn binary rebuilt and
  reinstalled (`go install ./cmd/djinn`), e.g. a criterion comparing
  `djinn init --print-lead` or `--print-contract` output against canon.
- `file-bead` — the fix is filing a bead, and `/create-bead` refuses to file
  because the repo's skill copies are stale (its compatibility guard asks for
  `djinn init --resync` or a djinn upgrade).
- `edit-seat-file` — the fix is an edit under `.djinn/seats/`, which workers
  never edit (contract §7).

The harness routes a `lead` finding to the lead and does not fail the bead on
it. It keeps its severity, `file` and `line`. If a worker could do any part of
the fix — code, a test, a doc, a commit, a proof run with the repo-built binary
(`go run ./cmd/djinn`) — it is `kind: "fix"`, not `lead`. Never use `lead` for
a finding you would rather not send to the fix step. The criterion row such a
finding blocks is `"status": "unverified"` with a `note` that opens
`lead action:` and names the action.

### Step 4. Pick the verdict

Pick it without `kind: "lead"` findings: a sidecar whose only BLOCKER or
IMPORTANT findings are `lead` findings is `SHIP`, or `SHIP-WITH-FIXES` when
other actionable findings remain.

- **`SHIP`** — no actionable findings at severity ≥ IMPORTANT. Note that a
  zero-findings `SHIP` on a non-trivial diff earns exactly one adversarial
  re-review before it is trusted, so do not reach for it to end the loop
  cheaply — reach for it when the code has actually earned it.
- **`SHIP-WITH-FIXES`** — ships once the listed BLOCKER/IMPORTANT findings are
  applied. This is the common verdict.
- **`REWORK`** — the approach itself is wrong; applying the listed fixes would
  not get there.

Do **not** invent findings to look thorough, and do not suppress a real one to
look agreeable. A truthful clean `SHIP` is a legitimate outcome.

### Step 5. Emit the sidecar

Emit a fenced ```json``` block as the **LAST** thing in your **visible** response
text — not inside a tool-result, not in a file. The harness extracts it from
your assistant text stream; a sidecar that never reaches visible text reads as a
parse failure and burns the loop's budget.


Field contract:

- `verdict` — exactly one of `SHIP`, `SHIP-WITH-FIXES`, `REWORK`.
- `severity_counts` — an object counting `BLOCKER`, `IMPORTANT`, `NIT`,
  `INVENTED`. The `BLOCKER` count here MUST equal the number of `BLOCKER`
  entries in `promoted_findings`; a mismatch is a structural fault and halts the
  loop.
- `invented_rate_pct` — `INVENTED` findings as a percentage of all findings
  (`0` when you found none).
- `criteria` — an array with **one entry per `acceptance_criteria` line**, in
  the bead's order, each `{index, status, file, line, note}`. Count lines the
  way the harness does: every non-blank line is one criterion. `index` is the
  1-based line number among those; `status` is exactly `pass`, `partial`,
  `fail` or `unverified` (lowercase); `file` and `line` cite the code or test
  that satisfies the criterion (for a `fail`, where the work belongs); `note`
  says in one sentence what you observed there. Before you mark a criterion
  `partial` or `fail` because it says `recorded in the evidence comment` or
  names a capture or measurement, open the prompt's `## Evidence on the bead` block and judge
  what its comments record; run no `bd` command for it. Proof found only there
  passes the criterion when it shows what the criterion asks, and the `note`
  names the comment (author and time). The harness copies each row onto the bead
  as its per-criterion evidence record, sets `evidence_failed` to the count of
  `partial` and `fail` rows, and sets `evidence_unverified` to the count of
  `unverified` rows. A sidecar missing a row for any line, or a row whose
  `status` is outside those four, is refused and the review re-runs — walk
  every line, including the ones about docs, tests and lint.

  **A check you cannot run is `unverified`, never graded.** When a criterion's
  check cannot run on your machine for an environment reason — a module proxy
  or network you cannot reach, a port you cannot bind, a tool not installed —
  first try the nearest check you can run (the installed tool's version,
  `go vet`, the package's own tests) and name it. Then write the row with
  `"status": "unverified"` and a `note` that opens `could not run:`, quotes the
  command and its error, and names the nearest check and its result. Such a row
  is never `partial` or `fail`, and the failure to run is never a BLOCKER or
  IMPORTANT finding: it says nothing about the work, and the operator decides.
  A check that runs and fails is graded as usual. A row whose only gap is a
  `kind: "lead"` finding is `unverified` too, with a `note` that opens
  `lead action:` and names the `lead_action` (Step 3).
- `suite` — `{revision, exit}` copied from the prompt's `## Test suite` block:
  the revision line (full, or abbreviated to at least 7 characters) and the
  exit code as a number. A sidecar whose `suite` is absent, or whose revision
  or exit differs from that block, is refused and the review re-runs. Omit it
  only when the prompt carries no `## Test suite` block. Every `criteria` row
  whose check is a test run names the suite run in its `note` (for example
  "the suite-run at 8fe8b9ae exited 0"), not a run of your own.
- `mutation_survivors` — an array of `{test, disposition, note}`, one entry per
  `survived` test in the prompt's `## Mutation check` report that you judge a
  guard (rubric 7). `test` is the report's `file:Name` (or bare `Name`),
  `disposition` is exactly `guard`, and `note` names the behaviour it pins. A
  survivor you do not accept as a guard is instead an IMPORTANT `kind: "fix"`
  finding citing its file. A sidecar that leaves a survivor with neither is
  refused and the review re-runs. Omit the array when there is no report or it
  names no survivor.
- `prior_findings` — an array of `{file, line, status, reason}`, one entry per
  finding the PREVIOUS iteration promoted and one per finding under
  `## Findings the fix step declined`, with `status` exactly `resolved`,
  `unresolved`, `upheld` or `withdrawn` (see "Answering the previous
  iteration"). `upheld` and `withdrawn` are for declined findings only and each
  needs a `reason`, one sentence on what the evidence showed; `reason` is
  optional on the other two. `upheld` counts as unresolved and `withdrawn` as
  resolved. Absent on iteration 1,
  where there is no previous review; an absent array on a later iteration reads
  as "no prior finding could be confirmed resolved". Each `unresolved` or
  `upheld` entry MUST have a matching `promoted_findings` row at the same
  citation; a `withdrawn` entry has none.
- `promoted_findings` — an array (possibly empty) of
  `{severity, kind, file, line, action, effort}`, plus `origin` from iteration 2
  on, `priority` on NIT `fix` findings and `caller_of_changed_code` on a caller
  finding (see Step 3). `kind` is `fix`, `counter` or `lead`. A `lead` finding
  also carries `lead_action`, exactly one of `reinstall-binary`, `file-bead` or
  `edit-seat-file` (Step 3); any other value reads as `kind: "fix"`. A `lead`
  finding still counts in `severity_counts`, but not in the `verdict`. `effort`
  is a rough size (`S` / `M` / `L`).
- `origin` — `"regression"` (the last fix introduced this finding) or
  `"latent"` (it pre-existed that fix). Omitted or unrecognized reads as
  `regression`. It decides whether an IMPORTANT holds the loop open or is filed
  as a P2 follow-up bead; a BLOCKER blocks under either origin. It applies only
  to findings NEW at their citation — a re-promotion of a finding the loop is
  already carrying, from any earlier pass, carries no origin, and any origin on
  one is ignored.
- `priority` — the per-finding filing grade for NIT `fix` findings: `"P4"`
  (report-only — the default, including the polish and absent-verification
  shapes), `"P3"` (a deferred behavior defect — report-only, below the P2
  floor), or `"P2"` (a deferred behavior defect severe enough to be carried on
  the backlog until fixed, worth a tracked `review-follow-up` bead — the ONLY
  grade that files), per the within-NIT rubric in Step 3. Optional and unused for
  BLOCKER/IMPORTANT (they route to the fix step, not the filer) and for
  counters; omit it or leave `""` there. An omitted or empty grade on a NIT
  falls back to the filer's batch default priority, which is below the P2 floor
  — an ungraded NIT is therefore report-only.

After the JSON is in your visible text, stop.

## Scope boundary

This skill judges **the diff**. It does NOT:

- Judge whether the bead was the right work to do (that is settled at filing, by `/create-bead`).
- Judge whether the bead's criteria are concrete enough to implement against
  (that is `/ac-quality-review`, which already ran before implementation).
- Render the bead's final acceptance verdict (that is `/verify-acceptance`,
  which runs after this loop on the settled tree).
- Apply its own findings (that is the loop's paired fix step).
